chunks: And by his chain, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
'A man cannot own his father, nor his mother, nor his paternal aunt, nor his maternal aunt; but he can own his brother, and others from his male relatives.'

key_terms.ذَوُو قَرَابَةٍ: those with kinship ties; relatives; used here to denote male relatives who can legally be owned
key_terms.وَالِدَ: father (in the context of close familial relations that are legally protected from ownership)
key_terms.يَمْلِكُ: to own/possess as property (in the juridical sense of ownership, specifically applied to the ownership of slaves in this context)

ai.seo_question: According to Imam al-Baqir, which family members can a man not own as slaves in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) establishes a legal ruling on the permissibility of owning close relatives as slaves. In the context of seventh-century Arabia where slavery was an existing institution, Islamic law placed restrictions on who could be enslaved. The ruling here specifies that one's direct ascendants and female relatives (father, mother, paternal aunt, maternal aunt) cannot legally be owned, while one's brother and other male relatives can be. This ruling reflects the Shia fiqh position on the manumission of relatives.

en.hubeali:
And by his chain, from Al Aa’la Bin Razeyn, from Muhammad Bin Muslim, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘The man can neither own his father, nor his mother, nor his paternal aunt, nor his maternal aunt; but he can own his brother, and others from ones with relationships from the men’.
